answer.question: My mom just turned 65 and is signing up for Medicare. How much will her Part B premium be each month in 2026, and is there anything that could make it higher?
answer.answer:
In 2026 the standard Part B premium is $202.90 a month, and most people pay that amount.

Two things could make your mom's premium higher:

1. **Higher income (IRMAA).** Medicare looks at the modified adjusted gross income on her IRS tax return from 2 years ago. For 2026, if her 2024 modified adjusted gross income was above $109,000 filing individually or $218,000 married filing jointly, she may pay an extra charge called the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA). You can learn more at Medicare.gov, and if she has to pay extra and disagrees (for example, her income is lower now because of a life event), she can visit SSA.gov/medicare/lower-irmaa.

2. **A late enrollment penalty.** If she doesn't sign up for Part B when she's first eligible, she may pay a late enrollment penalty for as long as she has Part B — her monthly premium may go up 10% for each period she could have had Part B but didn't sign up (the excerpt cuts off mid-sentence here).

If she has limited income and resources and needs help paying the premium, the handbook points to pages 91–92 for programs that may help. Separately, note the Part B deductible is $283 in 2026.

answer.question: Dad has Original Medicare and no other insurance. He spent 5 days in the hospital and then went straight into a skilled nursing facility for 30 days. What will he owe for that in 2026?
answer.answer:
Based on the handbook's 2026 amounts, and assuming both stays fall in the same benefit period (a benefit period starts when you're admitted and ends when you've had no inpatient hospital or skilled nursing care for 60 days in a row):

- Hospital, 5 days: he pays the $1,736 Part A deductible, then $0 each day for days 1–60.
- Skilled nursing facility (SNF), 30 days: he doesn't pay the deductible again, because he already paid it for the hospital care in the same benefit period. Days 1–20 are $0 each day; days 21–30 are $217 each day, which is $2,170 for those 10 days.

So his share works out to $1,736 + $2,170 = $3,906, plus Part B costs for doctors' services. If he also has Part B, Part B generally covers 80% of the Medicare-approved amount for doctors' services in the hospital, so he'd owe the rest of that. Medicare also doesn't cover extras like private-duty nursing, a TV or phone with a separate charge, personal care items, or a private room unless medically necessary.

Note: Medicare covers SNF care after a 3-day minimum medically necessary inpatient hospital stay (not counting the day he left the hospital), so a 5-day stay meets that. To check how benefit periods apply to his situation, see Medicare.gov/coverage/skilled-nursing-facility-care.

answer.question: What are the 2026 income and resource limits for qualifying for Extra Help with Medicare drug costs?
answer.answer:
The handbook doesn't list the 2026 limits. It gives the 2025 limits — you may qualify for Extra Help if your yearly income and resources are below these amounts in 2025: a single person, income less than $23,475 and resources less than $17,600; a married person living with a spouse and no other dependents, income less than $31,725 and resources less than $35,130 — and then says, "You can find 2026 income and resource limits on Medicare.gov."

Two other points: in some situations you may qualify even with higher income (for example, if you still work, live in Alaska or Hawaii, or have dependents living with you). Resources include money in a checking or savings account, stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and IRAs, but don't include your home, car, household items, burial plot, up to $1,500 for burial expenses (per person), or life insurance policies. Even if you don't think you qualify, you should still apply.

answer.question: My mom turns 65 on March 12. When can she sign up for Medicare without paying a penalty, and when would her coverage start?
answer.answer:
Because her birthday is March 12 (not the first of the month), your mom's Initial Enrollment Period is the 7-month period that begins 3 months before the month she turns 65 and ends 3 months after it — so December through June. Signing up during that window avoids a late enrollment penalty (in most cases, if you don't sign up for Part A, if you have to buy it, and Part B when first eligible, enrollment may be delayed and a penalty may be added to the monthly premium).

Coverage start depends on when she signs up:
- If she signs up during the first 3 months of her Initial Enrollment Period (December, January, or February), in most cases coverage begins the first day of her birthday month — March 1.
- If she signs up in March (the month she turns 65) or during the last 3 months (April, May, or June), coverage starts the first day of the month after she signs up.

Note that some people get Part A and Part B automatically; if she does, coverage starts the first day of the month she turns 65 and her Medicare card comes in the mail 3 months before her 65th birthday. For help with her specific situation, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY 1-877-486-2048.

answer.question: My husband is retiring in April and I'm 67 and covered by his employer's health plan. How long will I have to sign up for Part B, and does taking COBRA buy me more time?
answer.answer:
Because you're covered by a group health plan based on your husband's current employment, you get a Special Enrollment Period. You can sign up for Part B any time you're still covered by that plan, and during the 8-month period that begins the month after the employment ends or the coverage ends, whichever happens first. Signing up during a Special Enrollment Period usually means no late enrollment penalty.

COBRA does not buy you more time. COBRA isn't considered coverage based on current employment, so it doesn't count for this Special Enrollment Period — after coverage based on current employment ends you still have 8 months to sign up for Part B without a penalty, whether or not you choose COBRA. You generally aren't eligible for a Special Enrollment Period when the COBRA coverage ends, and if you have COBRA while eligible for Medicare, COBRA may only pay a small portion of your medical costs. To sign up, visit SSA.gov/medicare/sign-up.

answer.question: Mom has Original Medicare and nothing else. Is there a cap on what she can be charged out of pocket in a year, and would a Medicare Advantage plan cap it?
answer.answer:
No — with Original Medicare alone there's no yearly cap. The handbook says "There's no yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket if you have Original Medicare," though limits may apply if you add supplemental coverage like Medigap, Medicaid, or employer, retiree, or union coverage. (Under Original Medicare, if the Part B deductible — $283 in 2026 — applies, she pays all costs up to the Medicare-approved amount until she meets it, then typically 20% of the Medicare-approved amount.)

Yes — a Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C) would cap it. These plans "set a limit on what you'll have to pay out of pocket each year for services covered under Part A and Part B," and the limit may be different for in-network and out-of-network services. Once she reaches her plan's limit, she pays nothing for covered services for the rest of the year. Out-of-pocket costs and limits vary by plan, so check Medicare.gov/plan-compare or call the plans; your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) can also help compare costs. Separately, yearly out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by a Part D plan are capped at $2,100 in 2026.

She'd also still have other out-of-pocket costs when she gets care, such as any plan deductible and the copayment or coinsurance for each visit or service, which vary by plan and by whether the provider is in the plan's network.

answer.question: My father takes several expensive prescriptions. Is there any cap on what he'll have to pay for his drugs in 2026?
answer.answer: Yes. If your father has Medicare drug coverage (Part D), his yearly out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by his plan are capped at $2,100 in 2026. Once he reaches that limit — counting his own out-of-pocket spending plus certain payments other people or entities make, including Medicare's Extra Help program — he won't pay a copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year. Note that the cap applies to drugs his plan covers, and his costs before reaching it depend on things like his plan's deductible, the "tier" a drug is in, and which pharmacy he uses. He can also look at the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan, which spreads his out-of-pocket drug costs across the calendar year (January–December) — it helps with managing expenses but doesn't lower his drug costs. For specific plan costs, visit Medicare.gov/plan-compare or call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).

answer.question: Dad is 68, has had Medicare since he was 65 and never joined a drug plan because he takes no medication. If he joins one now, will he be charged a penalty, and how is it worked out?
answer.answer:
Most likely yes. Because he had no Medicare drug coverage (Part D) and no other "creditable" prescription drug coverage (drug coverage at least as good as Medicare's, such as from an employer or union, TRICARE, IHS, or VA) for 63 or more days in a row after his Initial Enrollment Period ended, he may have to pay a late enrollment penalty if he joins a drug plan now. Taking no medication doesn't excuse it — the handbook says even if you don't take drugs now, you should consider joining a plan when first eligible to avoid a penalty.

How it's worked out: the penalty is 1% of the "national base beneficiary premium" ($38.99 in 2026) multiplied by the number of full months he was eligible but went without Medicare drug coverage or other creditable coverage. The amount is rounded to the nearest $.10 and added to his monthly premium. So roughly three years (about 36 uncovered months) would be about 36% of $38.99. The base premium can change each year, so the penalty amount can go up or down, and he'll generally pay it for as long as he has Medicare drug coverage. If he gets Extra Help, he doesn't pay the penalty. After he joins, the plan will tell him whether he owes a penalty and what his premium will be. He should also keep and share records of any past creditable coverage — if he doesn't tell the plan about it, he may pay a penalty for as long as he has drug coverage.

To compare plans, visit Medicare.gov/plan-compare or call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) (see pages 114–117 or shiphelp.org).

answer.question: Dad is comparing Medigap Plan K and Plan L. What is the most each one would let him pay out of pocket in 2026, and how much of his costs do they cover?
answer.answer:
In 2026 the out-of-pocket yearly limit is $8,000 for Plan K and $4,000 for Plan L. Once he meets that limit and his yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), the Medigap plan pays 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year.

Before that, the two plans pay different shares of the gaps in Original Medicare. Plan K pays 50% and Plan L pays 75% of: the Part B coinsurance or copayment, the blood benefit (first 3 pints), the Part A hospice care coinsurance or copayment, the skilled nursing facility care coinsurance, and the Part A deductible — he pays the rest. Both pay 100% of Medicare Part A coinsurance and hospital costs (up to an additional 365 days after Medicare benefits are used). Neither covers the Part B deductible, Part B excess charges, or foreign travel emergency care.

answer.question: When is the best time for my dad to buy a Medigap policy, and what happens if he waits?
answer.answer:
The best time is during his Medigap Open Enrollment Period — a 6-month period that begins the first month he has Medicare Part B (Medical Insurance) and he's 65 or older. (Some states have additional Open Enrollment Periods.)

If he waits until after that period, he may not be able to buy a Medigap policy at all, or it may cost more. In certain situations he may still have the right to buy a policy outside that period — these are called guaranteed issue rights.

Two things to note: if he delays signing up for Part B because he has group health coverage based on his (or his spouse's) current employment, his Medigap Open Enrollment Period won't start until he gets Part B. For more help, he can call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) (phone numbers on pages 114–117) or his State Insurance Department, or visit Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans.

In the meantime, during the first 12 months he has Part B he can get the "Welcome to Medicare" preventive visit instead — he just needs to tell the doctor's office that's the visit he wants to schedule. He doesn't need to have had the "Welcome to Medicare" visit to later qualify for the yearly "Wellness" visit.

answer.question: Mom's doctor wants to set up home health care after her hip surgery. What will Medicare charge her for it, and does she have to be bedridden to qualify?
answer.answer:
She pays nothing for covered home health services. The one cost is for durable medical equipment (things like a walker or wheelchair) that Medicare covers as part of the care — for that she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, and the Part B deductible applies.

She does not have to be bedridden. Medicare covers home health as long as she needs part-time or intermittent skilled services and is "homebound," which means: she has trouble leaving home without help (like a cane, wheelchair, walker, crutches, special transportation, or another person) because of an illness or injury; leaving home isn't recommended because of her condition; or she's normally unable to leave home because it's a major effort.

Also required: a doctor or other health care provider (like a nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant) must assess her face-to-face before certifying she needs home health services, a doctor or other provider must order the care, and a Medicare-certified home health agency must provide it.

answer.question: Mom's cancer is terminal and her doctor brought up hospice. Who has to sign off before Medicare will cover it, and what would she have to pay?
answer.answer:
To qualify for hospice care, a hospice doctor and your mother's own doctor (if she has one) must certify that she's terminally ill — meaning a life expectancy of 6 months or less. She also has to sign a statement choosing hospice care (comfort care, also called palliative care) instead of other Medicare-covered treatments meant to cure her terminal illness and related conditions.

Costs: she pays nothing for hospice care, a copayment of up to $5 per prescription for outpatient drugs for pain and symptom management, and 5 percent of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite care (a short stay in a Medicare-approved facility, up to 5 days each time, so a caregiver can rest). Medicare won't pay room and board where she lives unless the hospice medical team decides she needs short-term inpatient care to manage pain and symptoms. Original Medicare is billed for hospice even if she's in a Medicare Advantage Plan. What she pays could differ if she has other coverage such as Medigap, Medicaid, or employer/union/retiree coverage — contact the plan with questions. For more on hospice and to find Medicare-approved providers, visit Medicare.gov/care-compare.

answer.question: My parents have Original Medicare. They're going to Portugal in June and to Puerto Rico in October. Would Medicare cover them if one of them ended up in the hospital on either trip?
answer.answer:
The two trips are treated differently.

Puerto Rico (October): For Medicare purposes Puerto Rico is part of the "U.S." — the handbook says the "U.S." includes the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa. With Original Medicare they can go to any Medicare-enrolled doctor, other health care provider, hospital, or other facility that accepts Medicare patients anywhere in the U.S., so a hospital stay there would be covered like one at home (they'd still pay their share of the cost).

Portugal (June): Medicare generally doesn't cover health care while you're traveling outside the U.S., though there are some limited exceptions — see Medicare.gov/coverage/travel-outside-the-u.s. to learn more. One exception: Medicare may cover medically necessary ambulance transportation to a foreign hospital only with admission for medically necessary covered inpatient hospital services; they'd pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount and the Part B deductible applies. The handbook also notes you may be able to buy a Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) policy that covers emergency care outside the U.S.

answer.question: Mom spent three nights in the hospital but the billing office says she was under observation the whole time, never admitted. She needs a skilled nursing facility now. Will Part A pay for it?
answer.answer:
Probably not, based on what you describe. Whether you're an inpatient or an outpatient "affects how much you pay for hospital services and if you qualify for Part A skilled nursing facility care." Your mom is counted as an outpatient if she was getting observation services — even if that included overnight stays — without a formal inpatient admission; she's an inpatient only when the hospital formally admits her with a doctor's order. The handbook also refers to a 3-day minimum inpatient hospital stay, so observation nights generally don't count toward it.

Two things worth checking:
- If she was under observation more than 24 hours, the hospital must give her a "Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice" ("MOON") explaining why she's an outpatient and how it affects what she pays for care after she leaves. You also now have appeal rights if a hospital changes her status from inpatient to outpatient, if certain conditions are met (see page 101, or Medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals-complaints/appeals/original-medicare).
- The 3-day minimum may not apply if her doctor participates in an Accountable Care Organization (ACO) approved for a Skilled Nursing Facility 3-Day Rule Waiver — ask her provider. Medicare Advantage Plans may also waive the 3-day stay; contact the plan.

answer.question: My father moved to the U.S. at 58 and has only about 6 years of work here. Does he have to pay for Part A, how much in 2026, and what happens if he puts it off?
answer.answer:
Most likely yes — he'd have to buy Part A. You normally get Part A with no monthly premium ("premium-free Part A") if you or your spouse paid Medicare taxes while working for a certain amount of time; if you aren't eligible for premium-free Part A, you may be able to buy it. If he buys it, in 2026 the premium is either $311 or $565 each month, depending on how long he or his spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes. In most cases, if he buys Part A he must also have Part B and pay monthly premiums for both (the standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90); if he chooses not to buy Part A, he can still buy Part B if he's eligible.

If he doesn't buy Part A when first eligible, his monthly premium may go up 10%, and he'd pay the higher premium for twice the number of years he could have had Part A but didn't sign up — for example, 2 years without signing up means a 10% higher premium for 4 years.

The handbook doesn't spell out how many years of work are needed, so to confirm his exact situation and premium amount, he can visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE. If he needs help paying the Part A premium, see pages 91–92.

answer.question: Mom is in a Medicare Advantage plan and wants to move to a different one for next year. When can she make that change, and when would the new plan kick in?
answer.answer:
She has two main chances to switch Medicare Advantage plans:

1. Open Enrollment, October 15 to December 7 — she can join, switch, or drop a Medicare Advantage Plan for the next year. Coverage starts January 1, as long as the plan gets her enrollment request by December 7.

2. The Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, January 1 to March 31 — if she's already in a Medicare Advantage Plan, she can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage). She can only make one change during this period, and the new coverage starts the first day of the month after the plan gets her request.

Outside those periods she generally can't change plans during the year, though a Special Enrollment Period may apply in certain situations, like if she moves or loses other insurance coverage. There's also a 5-star Special Enrollment Period (December 8 to November 30 the following year) if a plan with a 5-star quality rating is available in her area. For help comparing plans, she can call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), TTY 1-877-486-2048, or contact her State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at shiphelp.org.

answer.question: Mom's house burned in a wildfire and in the chaos she missed her Medicare sign-up window. Is there any way for her to enroll now, and how soon after that could she get a drug plan?
answer.answer: Yes — the handbook describes a Special Enrollment Period for people who missed signing up because of an "exceptional circumstance." If she signs up for Part A or Part B during a Special Enrollment Period because of an exceptional circumstance, she then has 2 months to join a Medicare drug plan (Part D) or a Medicare Advantage Plan with or without drug coverage, and that coverage starts the first day of the month after the plan gets her request to join. (The handbook doesn't list which situations count as exceptional circumstances, so she should check with the plan or Medicare.gov, or call her State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) — phone numbers are on pages 114–117.) If instead she signs up for Part B during the General Enrollment Period (January 1 – March 31), she can also join a drug plan then, with 2 months after signing up for Part B to do so, and drug coverage starting the month after the plan gets her request. One thing to keep in mind: a late enrollment penalty can apply if there's a period of 63 or more days in a row without Medicare drug coverage or other creditable drug coverage.

answer.answer: Yes. Because she's already in a Medicare Advantage Plan, she can use the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, which runs January 1 to March 31 each year. During that time she can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage), or drop the plan and return to Original Medicare — and if she returns to Original Medicare she can also join a separate Medicare drug plan. She can only make one change during this period, and the new coverage starts the first of the month after the plan gets her request. Note that during this period she couldn't later switch from Original Medicare back into a Medicare Advantage Plan, join a separate drug plan if she's in Original Medicare, or switch from one Medicare drug plan to another. One more thing to check: if she first became eligible for Medicare recently and joined during her Initial Enrollment Period, she can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan or go back to Original Medicare within the first 3 months she has Medicare.

answer.question: Mom is down to two Medicare Advantage plans, an HMO and a PPO. Would she have to pick a primary care doctor or get referrals, and what happens if she sees a doctor outside the network?
answer.answer:
The two plan types work differently:

**HMO:** In most cases she would have to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases she'd need a referral to see a specialist (some services, like yearly mammogram screenings, don't require a referral). She generally must get care from providers in the plan's network — except for emergency care, out-of-area urgent care, or temporary out-of-area dialysis, which are covered in or out of network. If she gets non-emergency care outside the network without authorization, she may have to pay the full cost. Some HMOs, called HMO Point-of-Service (HMOPOS) Plans, may let her get some out-of-network services for a higher copayment or coinsurance.

**PPO:** She does not need to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases does not need a referral for a specialist. She can use out-of-network ("non-plan") specialists, but her costs for covered services will usually be lower if she uses in-network ones — because certain PPO providers are "preferred," she can save money by using them.

Also, if a doctor or other provider leaves an HMO's network, the plan will notify her and she may choose another network doctor. For details on either plan, check with the plan or visit Medicare.gov.

answer.question: Mom has a high income and gets her drug coverage through a Medicare Advantage plan. Does she still owe the Part D extra charge, and does she pay it to the plan?
answer.answer:
Yes. If her income is above the limit (in 2026 it's $109,000 if she files individually or $218,000 if married filing jointly), she pays an extra amount on top of her plan premium — sometimes called "Part D IRMAA" — and the handbook says this applies even if she's in a Medicare Advantage Plan that includes drug coverage.

She does not pay it to the plan. Usually Medicare or the Railroad Retirement Board (RRB) deducts the extra amount from her Social Security or RRB payment. If Medicare or the RRB bills her instead, she must pay the extra amount to Medicare or the RRB, not her plan. She pays Part D IRMAA separately even if an employer or another third party (like a retirement system) pays her plan premiums. If she doesn't pay it, she could lose her Medicare drug coverage (Part D), might not be able to join another plan right away, and may owe a late enrollment penalty added to her monthly premium for as long as she has drug coverage.

answer.question: Dad's drug plan puts his medicine on an expensive tier and his doctor says the cheaper ones won't work for him. Can he ask the plan to charge him less, and how does that work?
answer.answer:
Yes — he can ask his plan for an "exception" (a request that the plan bend its own rules in his case). If his drug is on a higher tier and his prescriber (his doctor or other provider legally allowed to write prescriptions) thinks he needs that drug instead of a similar drug on a lower tier, he or his prescriber can ask the plan for an exception to get a lower coinsurance or copayment for the higher tier drug. In particular, he can ask for an exception if he thinks he should pay less for a higher tier drug because he or his prescriber believe he can't take any of the lower tier drugs for the same condition.

How it works: he or his prescriber must contact the plan to ask for a coverage determination or exception. The plan's written decision about how much he pays is called a "coverage determination." If he hasn't gotten the prescription yet, he or his prescriber may make a standard request or an expedited (fast) request by phone or in writing; if he's asking to be paid back for drugs he already bought, the plan can require the standard request in writing (an expedited request can be made by calling or writing the plan). The request will be expedited if he hasn't gotten the prescription and the plan determines, or his prescriber tells the plan, that his life or health may be at risk by waiting. If a network pharmacy can't fill the prescription, the pharmacist gives him a notice explaining how to contact the plan to make the request — if not, he should ask for a copy. More information: Medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals-complaints/appeals/drug-plans.

answer.question: Dad is choosing between Medigap Plan N and a high-deductible Plan G. What extra out-of-pocket costs does each of those carry in 2026?
answer.answer:
The handbook's Medigap chart for 2026 shows these differences:

**Plan N** — It pays 100% of the Part B coinsurance, but you must pay a copayment of up to $20 for some office visits and up to a $50 copayment for emergency room visits that don't result in an inpatient admission. Like Plan G, Plan N doesn't cover the Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), and it doesn't cover Part B excess charges (the extra amount a doctor who doesn't accept Medicare's approved amount can charge).

**High-deductible Plan G** — Plans F and G also offer a high-deductible version in some states. With it, you must pay Medicare-covered costs (coinsurance, copayments, and deductibles) up to the deductible amount of $2,950 in 2026 before your policy pays anything.

For specific policy prices and what's sold in his state, he can call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) — phone numbers are on pages 114–117 of the handbook.

answer.question: Dad has had a Medigap policy for years but wants to try a Medicare Advantage plan. If he hates it, can he get his Medigap policy back?
answer.answer: Maybe — it depends on timing and his state's rules. If he drops a Medigap policy to join a Medicare Advantage Plan for the first time, he has a single 12-month "trial right period" to get his Medigap policy back if the same insurance company still sells it once he returns to Original Medicare. If that policy isn't available, he can buy certain Medigap policies, depending on state law and whether he was new to Medicare on or after January 1, 2020. Outside that trial right period, he may not be able to get the same policy back — or in some cases any Medigap policy — or he might have to pay more, depending on his state's Medigap enrollment rules and his situation. Also note that he can't buy Medigap while in a Medicare Advantage Plan unless he's switching back to Original Medicare, and most Medigap policies don't cancel automatically, so he'd need to contact his insurance company to cancel. For more, he can call his State Insurance Department (content.naic.org/state-insurance-departments), visit Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans, or call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).

answer.question: How much would a Medigap Plan G policy cost my dad per month?
answer.answer:
The handbook doesn't list Medigap premiums — there's no set price for Plan G. Medigap is sold by private insurance companies, and you pay a monthly premium to the company in addition to the monthly Part B premium you pay to Medicare. The handbook notes that "The costs can vary between plans offered by different companies for exactly the same coverage, and may go up as you get older," and that some states limit Medigap premium costs. Also, a Medigap policy only covers one person, so your dad would need his own policy.

To find actual prices for Plan G where your dad lives, use the Medigap plan finder at Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans, and you can review the booklet "Choosing a Medigap Policy: A Guide to Health Insurance for People with Medicare" at Medicare.gov/publications. One timing note: the best time to buy is during his Medigap Open Enrollment Period — the 6-month period beginning the first month he has Medicare Part B and is 65 or older — because after that he may not be able to buy a policy or it may cost more.
